headline: From fire hazard to green gold
text:
When forests are managed sustainably, they can provide more than resources—they can create livelihoods, strengthen communities and preserve cultural heritage.


1. Nawalpur, Nepal — A Forest at Risk

  • In Binayi Triveni, Nawalpur District, forest debris such as dry leaves, branches and undergrowth contributed to wildfire risk.

  • Local women saw an opportunity to turn this problem into a resource.

2. Meet Meena Poudel

  • Meena Poudel, 41, Secretary of the Binayi Community Forest User Group, helps lead the initiative.

  • Women collect forest biomass that would otherwise remain on the forest floor and fuel fires.

3. From Forest Waste to Fertiliser

  • Collected branches and biomass are shredded and placed in compost windrows.

  • The material is turned and monitored for moisture and temperature for about 90 days.

  • Beneficial microorganisms are added to produce organic biofertiliser.

4. Turning Risk into Business

  • The enterprise now produces more than 60,000 kg of fertiliser each year.

  • The group aims to increase production to 125,000 kg annually.

  • Biomass is collected by the women themselves or purchased locally, creating additional income opportunities.

5. Impact on Forests and Farmers

  • The initiative has contributed to a reported 70% reduction in forest fires over the past year.

  • Farmers are using the organic fertiliser as an alternative to chemical inputs.

  • The compost is intended to improve soil health, fertility and microbial biodiversity.

6. Women Driving Local Change

  • The enterprise provides income opportunities for approximately 400 people.

  • Women are using their earnings to support household needs, including children's education.

  • The group is also working to develop skills and increase women's participation in leadership.

7. From Local Action to Wider Support

  • The local municipality matched the group's initial capital.

  • In 2023, FAO's Forest and Farm Facility (FFF) provided USD 25,000 in catalytic funding.

  • Support included training, business planning, market analysis, quality standards and networking.

8. Scaling the Model

  • What began in one community forest now reaches six forests.

  • The group plans to expand its work to 42 forests.

  • Its approach links wildfire prevention, women's livelihoods, sustainable forest management and soil health.

Closing Message

Forest waste becomes fertiliser. Fire risk becomes opportunity. And local women become drivers of a more resilient forest-based economy.

headline: Woodcarving empowers women in Nepal
text:
1. A Forest-Based Community

Piple-Pokhara, Makwanpur

  • In the foothills of Makwanpur, forests are central to local livelihoods.

  • Families depend on timber and non-timber forest products, including fruits and medicinal plants.

  • For women, however, opportunities to earn an income have historically been limited.

StoryMap focus: A community where forests provide both livelihoods and possibilities.

2. A New Opportunity for Women

Learning the craft

  • About ten years ago, women from the community joined woodcarving training supported by the Forest and Farm Facility (FFF) and Piple-Pokhara CFUG.

  • 50 women completed initial training, with 30 receiving advanced training.

  • The women also received woodcarving machinery.

Key milestone: 2017 — Shramjivi Women Handicraft Enterprise is established.

3. Turning Wood Waste into Products

From forest resources to handicrafts

  • The women began producing photo frames, keyrings, Nepal-themed maps and other wooden crafts.

  • Piple-Pokhara CFUG provided soft wood, wood scraps and a workshop.

  • Using available wood and offcuts also helped reduce material that could otherwise contribute to forest-fire risk.

StoryMap message: What was once waste became a resource for livelihoods.

4. Women as Forest Stewards

Livelihoods and conservation go hand in hand

  • Environmental restrictions limited collection of wood directly from local forests.

  • Instead, the enterprise used permitted soft wood, forest litter and sawmill offcuts.

  • This connected women's entrepreneurship with sustainable forest management, restoration and fire prevention.

5. Overcoming Challenges

Keeping the enterprise alive

  • The enterprise faced high turnover as women left because of marriage, social pressures and the demanding nature of handicraft production.

  • Additional FFF support from 2024–2025 focused on strengthening the business.

  • Women received support in:

    • Technical carving

    • Business planning

    • Financial literacy

    • Marketing

    • Product development

6. Opening New Markets

From local craft to growing demand

  • Four community forests agreed to supply raw materials at reduced prices.

  • Private sawmills committed to provide offcuts.

  • Local businesses agreed to help sell the handicrafts.

  • New products included Theki, bowls, trays, wine glasses and Okhal.

Visual opportunity: Show the products alongside the locations of suppliers, workshops and markets.

7. A Growing Source of Income

Skills translated into earnings

  • Women now earn approximately NPR 10,000–15,000 per month (USD 70–105).

  • Products reach local, regional and provincial markets, including Kathmandu Valley.

  • Local governments also purchase the handicrafts as gifts and tokens of appreciation.

Key message: Skills, forests and markets are creating new economic opportunities for women.

8. Preserving Heritage, Building the Future

A model for community forestry

  • Woodcarving provides more than income: it strengthens women's confidence and preserves traditional Nepali craftsmanship.

  • The enterprise demonstrates how forest resources can support women-led businesses while contributing to conservation.

  • Piple-Pokhara offers a model that could be adapted by other community forests across Nepal.

Closing StoryMap Message

headline: Award-winning coffee transforms lives in Nepal
text:
Strengthening Coffee Production

  • The Coffee Cooperative Union Limited (CCUL) supports 12 cooperatives and 473 members in Nepal.

  • Support from the Forest and Farm Facility (FFF) in 2024–25 helped CCUL improve coffee production, processing, and marketing.

  • CCUL established six nurseries to produce healthy seedlings, targeting 50,000 seedlings annually.

  • Farmers are adopting coffee-based agroforestry, including banana and Nepalese alder trees for shade.

Building Farmers’ Skills

  • CCUL developed standard procedures for coffee production, processing, and marketing.

  • 679 farmers received refresher training in:

    • Coffee farming technologies

    • Post-harvest handling and processing

    • Climate-resilient practices

  • A locally adapted cultivation calendar helps farmers plan activities, reduce crop losses, improve productivity, and respond to unpredictable weather.

  • Exposure visits enabled farmers to learn from other coffee producers.

  • Members can now produce around 20 tonnes of export-quality green coffee beans.

From Beans to a Branded Product

  • FFF support provided CCUL with a modern roasting machine capable of processing up to 3 tonnes of roasted coffee annually.

  • Under the Sindu Organic Coffee brand, roasting increases the product’s value from USD 10/kg for green beans to USD 20/kg.

  • CCUL opened the Beautiful Café in Sukute, creating jobs for two local women involved in roasting, packaging, marketing, and barista services.

Expanding Markets and Recognition

  • CCUL secured supply agreements with international buyers in Korea and Japan, alongside several domestic companies.

  • Its coffee has received recognition and awards from Nepal’s National Tea and Coffee Development Board and the Nepal Coffee Producers Association.

Inclusive Economic Opportunities

  • More than half of CCUL members are women or youth, while about one-quarter are Indigenous or Dalit people.

  • The initiative creates opportunities across the coffee value chain—from growing and processing to packaging and café services.

  • Overall, FFF support has strengthened skills, incomes, market access, local employment, and community leadership, benefiting CCUL members from bean to cup.

headline: Turning leaves into livelihoods
text:
Appropriate technology, traditional knowledge and women-led enterprise can create income while supporting a cleaner, more sustainable environment.
For generations, women in Nepal have crafted **dunatapari**—traditional plates and bowls made from Sal leaves stitched with bamboo fibres. In Dangisharan Rural Municipality, **21 women** of the Milijuli Tilakanya Dunatapri Udhyami Firm are turning this traditional skill into a stronger livelihood. With support from the **Forest and Farm Facility (FFF)**, their cooperative introduced a custom-made machine that uses heat and pressure to shape leaves into different-sized plates. The new technology has **tripled production**, enabling the women to produce more than **108,000 plates in one year** and earn **NPR 155,640 (about USD 1,150)**. Improved packaging and access to new markets have further strengthened their enterprise. The biodegradable plates are increasingly used at **restaurants, hotels, weddings, pujas, schools, fairs and local government events**, providing a sustainable alternative to single-use plastics. The initiative demonstrates how **appropriate technology, traditional knowledge and women-led enterprise** can create income while supporting a cleaner, more sustainable local environment.
